verses.1:
Al-Mizan holds that the disconnected letters combine those opening chapters that begin alifilām mīm and those beginning alifilām rāʾ, reflecting a combination of the teachings in those two groups of chapters.

In context, “These are the signs (āyāt) of the Book” refers primarily to observable cosmic signs of monotheism—such as the heavens, earth, sun, and moon—which, when contemplated, yield certainty about the origin of the cosmos, the return to God, and the truth of the revelation. The Book is thus the universal book of the cosmos, in one sense the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ); alternatively, it may be the Qurʾan insofar as it figuratively contains cosmic signs.

The verse consequently joins natural evidence, embodied in the cosmos, with verbal evidence, embodied in the Qurʾan. “But most people do not believe” qualifies both: they disbelieve in the tangible signs and in the revealed truth. The distant demonstrative pronoun (tilka) marks the high rank of the cosmic signs, which decisively show God’s oneness and exclusive lordship. “The truth” (al-ḥaqq) is exclusive: what was sent down to the Prophet is pure truth, neither falsehood nor a mixture of truth and falsehood. The wording also carries blame and reproof.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as evidence for God’s sole lordship over the cosmos. The heavens stand above the earth without visible tangible pillars; the sun and moon are subjugated within a continuous order and move to a specified term. These realities require one who raises, preserves, governs, and orders them: God, the only Lord.

The heavens’ elevation means their separation from the earth, through which they overshadow it and bring such things as rays, rain, and lightning. Their stability, like that of the earth, depends absolutely on God’s power and will through causes assigned by His permission. Even if visible pillars supported them, this would not make them independent of God. The phrase does not absolutely deny pillars, but denies visible ones. It is meant to awaken people from their habitual neglect of familiar causal connections: unusual phenomena, such as elevated celestial bodies without visible supports, impel the innate nature to seek their cause and thus lead it to God.

This does not mean that matters whose causes are known cease to depend on God, while unknown matters depend on Him directly. The Qurʾan affirms both that everything besides God is created by and dependent on Him, and that causality is constant. A ceiling supported by a pillar and a celestial body standing through its particular nature or general gravitation alike stand through their respective causes by God’s permission.

The verse’s chief aim is not to prove a Creator, but to establish the oneness of lordship. The polytheists addressed already acknowledged one Creator and Originator, but held that He had delegated the administration of particular domains—such as heaven, earth, life, death, war, and peace—to powerful beings whose favor should be sought. The unified governance of the cosmos, expressed by God’s presiding over the Throne and disposing the sun and moon, refutes this by showing that its Lord and Master is one. Thus the raising of the heavens is a prelude to the argument from comprehensive governance.

“Without any pillars” modifies their raising, while “that you see” describes the pillars; the interpretation that “you can see” begins an independent sentence is unlikely, unless “the heavens” includes the entire visible upper region. “Each moving for a specified term” may refer to the sun and moon individually, but more likely includes the heavens as well, since motion applies continually to all of them.

“He directs the command” means that He arranges diverse things in their proper places and succession so that each reaches its intended benefit and perfection without disorder. His universal management directs all things toward their particular ends and toward the collective end: return to God and the life of the Hereafter after this worldly life.

The elaborated signs are, apparently, cosmic signs, whose elaboration is God’s differentiation and separation of things and the extraction of what lies concealed in them: light from darkness, truth from falsehood, good from evil, and ultimately the righteous from the corrupt and the rewarded from the punished. This is why the verse connects them to certainty of encountering one’s Lord: the Day of Meeting is also the Day of Separation. The common interpretation that the signs are scriptural signs explained in revealed books is possible, but less consistent with the chapter’s theme and immediate context. The explicit phrase “your Lord,” rather than “Him,” further emphasizes that the Creator and Governor of the world is also the listeners’ sole Lord.
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains rawāsī as firmly fixed mountains. Zawj means a pair and may refer to the pair collectively or to either member; zawjayn ithnayn emphasizes two rather than four.

God’s spreading of the earth means expanding it so that animals can live on it and crops and trees can grow. The sequence of earth, fixed mountains, streams, fruits, and the alternation of night and day displays a connected design for human and animal habitation. Were the earth merely flat, its water reserves would not emerge to irrigate crops and orchards. God placed mountains, stored within them what descends from the sky, brought forth rivers and springs to irrigate the land, and thereby produced varied fruits. Heat and cold contribute to ripening, growth, expansion, and contraction, while light and darkness regulate creatures’ movement, their search for sustenance, and their rest.

This ordered connection—earth enabling mountains, mountains enabling rivers, rivers enabling fruits, and night and day completing the intended benefit—indicates one uniquely wise Manager with no partner in lordship. The signs are therefore for those who reflect.

“Of every fruit He has made in it two kinds” means that fruits occur in differing varieties, such as summer and winter, sweet and otherwise, moist and dry. The dual here can express repeated differentiation, not necessarily two varieties only. Al-Ṭanṭāwī’s interpretation of the phrase as male and female organs in plants states undisputed scientific facts, but Al-Mizan judges it unsupported by the verse’s apparent wording: the verse says that fruits are of two kinds, not that they were made from two mates. Such pairing may be inferred from other verses, but not from this wording. The view that it combines male and female with further differences, making four individuals, is likewise unpersuasive.

“He draws the night’s cover over the day” means that God covers daylight with the darkness of night, so that the illuminated sky becomes dark. The claim that each of night and day covers the other lacks supporting evidence. Reflection on this precise, mutually compatible system reveals a single Lord, free from ignorance and incapacity, who cares for all things and guides human beings toward their everlasting happiness.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan explains ṣinwān as date palms growing from a common root, while ghayr ṣinwān denotes those with separate roots; ukul is what is eaten from a tree. The verse points to adjacent, similar tracts of land containing vineyards, varied crops, and date palms from common or separate roots, all watered by the same water, yet differing in form, color, taste, quantity, and other desirable qualities. This is evidence that the cosmic order rests on the intentional design of a wise transcendent Creator, to whom things submit by their natures and according to His will.

The objection that such differences arise from each thing’s inherent nature or from external influences does not end the inquiry. One must ask why the internal and external causes themselves differ, and then seek the cause of that difference. This regress reaches a fundamental physical substance uniform in its parts, which cannot explain the diversity of forms and effects. There must therefore be a supreme cause beyond all other causes, which brings the substance of the universe into being and manifests it in diverse forms and effects. It is a single cause possessing consciousness and will; without diversity in its wills, things would have no distinguishing features.

Attributing these differences to diverse divine wills does not deny causality. God’s will is not like human will, an incidental quality whose changes alter the essence. Rather, these various wills are His active attribute, abstracted from the complete causes and reasons of things; their variation does not entail variation in the divine essence. Because the argument depends on such intellectual premises, the verse addresses those who apply reason.

Just as the preceding verses attribute the raising of the heavens, the spreading of the earth, and the formation of mountains and rivers directly to God while omitting intermediate causes, this verse directly attributes differences in foodstuffs to Him in order to awaken the innate understanding to seek the ultimate cause. The shift from “He” to the majestic “We” in “We give some of them an advantage over others in flavor” identifies God Himself as that real cause. The first-person expression together with the third-person discourse also implies divine causes beneath God that act by His command and return ultimately to Him.

The argument establishes the unity of God’s lordship, not merely the existence of a Creator or the unity of the Divine Essence. Diverse effects arising from a common origin require a cause beyond their shared nature, while their order reveals His will and plan; hence God is their planner and sole Lord. The passage addresses polytheists who accepted God’s unity in essence but posited many lords, not alleged pre-Islamic Arab atheists, for the context supplies no evidence for the latter reading.

The argument of (13:3) proceeds from unity in multiplicity: the interconnected management of diverse things points to one Manager. That of (13:4) proceeds from multiplicity in unity: differing effects and properties in things with one origin show that their initiator transcends their natures and their subordinate causes. The argument of (13:2) combines both perspectives: the dispersed world is under one system of management, while its details disclose multiplicity emerging from unity and the separation of things. Its reference to God’s differentiation of signs, truth and falsehood, and the fortunate and unfortunate also points to Resurrection and Final Judgment; therefore it concludes with certainty of encountering one’s Lord.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse turns, after the preceding establishment of monotheism, prophethood, and resurrection through the signs of creation, to the disbelievers’ doubt about resurrection. Their question—whether, after becoming dust (turāb), they can be a new creation—is itself the proper object of wonder. The form “If you are to wonder” indicates that astonishment at such an evidently false statement is unavoidable for a rational person.

Their objection assumes that, once the bodily structure of flesh, bones, organs, and physical capacities decomposes into dust, the human being has ceased to exist and cannot be created anew. The commentary distinguishes three aspects of this doubt. First, if they deny that dust can become a complete human being, the successive transformation of earthly material into semen, a clinging mass, flesh, and a human body establishes that such transformation is possible (22:5). Second, if they deny existence after non-existence, re-creation is possible just as the first creation was possible (36:78-79). Third, if they claim that no enduring subject remains to receive the new creation, the Qur’an teaches that the human being is not merely the changing body but a higher spirit (rūḥ), or soul (nafs), joined to and acting through it.

The soul preserves personal identity despite bodily change. Death is God’s taking of the soul and severing of its bodily connection; resurrection is the renewal of the body and the soul’s reunion with it, so that the person stands before God for judgment. Thus, people do not vanish into the earth: the angel of death takes the souls designated by “you” and “I,” preserves them, and they are returned to God when reunited with their bodies (32:10-11).

Accordingly, human life is not confined to this transient world but continues in an everlasting abode. Its happiness depends on what one acquires here through faith and good deeds: following truth and believing God’s signs brings enduring felicity and nearness to God, whereas attachment to the earth and turning from the reminder leads to permanent misery and to the Fire.

The verse’s condemnation and punishment are therefore not merely a threat addressed to speakers of the objection; they are necessary consequences of their belief. To hold that death extinguishes human personality is to reduce the person to bodily life alone and, in reality, to deny the divine world, since lordship without a return to the Lord is meaningless. This belief turns one from everlasting felicity toward worldly and material aims, leaving one unable to strive for nearness to God, like a person in chains. It also ruins the means of happiness and produces abiding misery. Thus, “They are the ones who defy their Lord” denotes their turning from the divine and everlasting realm; the collars (aghlāl) denote their bondage to earthly desire, ignorance, denial, and disbelief; and their abiding in the Fire denotes their everlasting torment and misery.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers “press” the Prophet for evil because, mockingly, they demand the threatened divine punishment rather than asking for mercy and compassion. The exemplary punishments (mathulāt) are the deterrent calamities that destroyed earlier nations for rejecting their messengers. Their demand is therefore astonishing: they seek punishment despite knowing what befell those before them.

“Indeed your Lord is forgiving to mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed your Lord is severe in retribution” may be an independent statement or one explaining why their conduct is so strange. God’s mercy encompasses people even amid wrongdoing, while His retribution is severe; yet His mercy precedes His wrath. Why, then, do they turn from forgiveness and hasten toward punishment? The expression “your Lord” also indicates that these polytheists and idolaters do not take God as their Lord, whereas the Prophet does.

The forgiveness and punishment intended here are not restricted to the afterlife, since the idolaters sought worldly punishment and the cited exemplary punishments were worldly. God’s mercy and forgiveness likewise extend beyond the Day of Resurrection: He may forgive whomever He wills, even a wrongdoer, when wisdom requires, and He may punish, as indicated by ‘If You punish them, they are indeed Your creatures; but if You forgive them, You are indeed the All-mighty, the All-wise’ (5:118).

Because the verse says that God is forgiving “to mankind,” rather than only to believers or penitents, anyone who turns to His mercy and seeks forgiveness may be forgiven, whether believer or disbeliever and whether the sin is major or minor. Polytheism, however, is not forgiven while it remains polytheism: one who asks forgiveness for it thereby turns to monotheism and becomes a believer. This is the restriction stated in: Indeed Allah does not forgive that any partner should be ascribed to Him, but He forgives anything besides that to whomever He wishes (4:48). The disbelievers should therefore have hastened to seek forgiveness for idolatry and its consequences by giving priority to faith in God and His Messenger, or sought worldly goods such as health, comfort, wealth, and offspring, which God may grant even to wrongdoers who neither believe nor submit. Forgiveness cannot coexist with wrongdoing insofar as the wrongdoer persists in it.

The commentary notes that the Arabic construction is literally “possessed of forgiveness” (la dhū maghfira), apparently avoiding the implication that forgiveness is actively bestowed on every wrongdoer while he remains in wrongdoing. It means that God possesses forgiveness for people and may apply it when beneficial; alternatively, human wrongdoing does not compel Him to abandon forgiveness altogether. Although Muʿtazilī and other Sunnī theologians disputed the verse’s scope, Al-Mizan holds its meaning to be absolute, restricted only by the exclusion of ascribing partners to God in (4:48).
verses.7:
Al-Mizan explains that the faithless are not requesting the decisive sign of punishment mentioned earlier; rather, while slighting the Qurʾan, they demand an additional miracle to prove the Prophet’s mission, like those given to earlier prophets. Their demand assumes, wrongly, that a Messenger must possess unrestricted supernatural power and supply whatever sign people demand.

The reply is addressed to the Prophet rather than commanded for delivery to them, suggesting that their lack of understanding does not deserve a direct answer. He is a human being sent to warn of God’s punishment, arrogance in refusing worship, and corruption on earth. He possesses no independent harm or benefit, death, life, or resurrection, and his duty is only to convey his Lord’s message; signs belong to God, who sends them as He wills.

Thus, although the Qurʾan—the best sign—is before them, the Prophet’s role is to guide by warning. In accordance with God’s constant way of directing creatures toward their perfection and what benefits them in this world and the next, every people has a guide to the truth. The earth is never without such a guide, whether a warning prophet or another guide acting by God’s command.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan takes “what every female carries,” “what the wombs reduce (mā taʿghīḍu al-arḥām),” and “what they increase” as three functions of the womb in pregnancy: the fetus it bears and protects, the menstrual blood stored and used to nourish the fetus, and blood it expels, such as postpartum blood or spotting during pregnancy. This interpretation is supported by reports from the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household and is also sometimes attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās. Interpretations that make reduction and increase refer to a pregnancy’s duration—whether relative to nine months, six months, miscarriage, or a maximum term—lack a contextual clue for this figurative use of “reduction.”

“Everything is by measure (bi-miqdār) with Him” explains God’s knowledge of these matters. A measure is the defining limit by which an existing thing is distinguished; without such a limit, it would not exist. Since every thing has a divinely fixed boundary it cannot exceed, and nothing escapes God’s knowledge, He necessarily knows all that wombs carry, reduce, and increase. The verse consequently reinforces that signs belong to the all-knowing, all-powerful Lord, not to the Messenger, who is only a warner.

The commentary holds that the sensible (al-shahāda) and the Unseen (al-ghayb) are relative terms: something is sensible to what falls within its limits of perception and unseen to what lies beyond them. Knowledge is a kind of encompassment, so no bounded being can encompass what is outside its existential limits. God alone knows the Unseen absolutely, because He is not limited and encompasses all things; in truth, nothing is unseen to Him.

God is the All-great, possessing and encompassing every perfection and more, and the All-sublime, above and dominant over everything with the utmost highness. These names explain why sensible and unseen things are equally known to Him: He encompasses and dominates all things, while nothing can dominate, overcome, or be concealed from Him.

verses.10: Al-Mizan explains sāribun bi al-nahār as one who openly follows his path by day. Since God knows the sensible and the Unseen alike, secret and public speech are equal before Him, as are one who conceals himself and his plotting in the night and one who travels openly by day. Neither hidden conversations nor nocturnal concealment escapes His knowledge.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan holds that the pronouns in the verse refer to the human being mentioned in the preceding verse, not to God, the Prophet, or the one openly visible by day. The muʿaqqibāt, derived from taʿqīb, are angels who circulate before and behind a person as he travels toward his Lord. “Before” and “behind” therefore extend beyond spatial directions to everything surrounding a human being in his bodily and spiritual journey: physical circumstances, past and forthcoming states, nearness and distance, happiness and misery, deeds, and the reward or punishment stored for him.

A human being is a soul and body, with the soul as the principal reality: it feels and wills, receives commands and prohibitions, is the locus of faith and disbelief, and bears reward, punishment, happiness, and misery. The body is its instrument. Since people possess neither independent benefit or harm nor power over their own preservation, God protects them and all connected with them through angels. Without this protection, destruction would encompass them.

The angels act only by God’s command. Since both preservation and destruction, permanence and annihilation, are effected only by His command, they guard a person not merely “by” God’s command but also from a command of God that would otherwise bring destruction or change. All affairs thus belong to God and return to Him. The verse expounds the preceding statement that everything is by measure with Him: people and all that pertains to them are preserved within a divinely ordered system until another divine command changes their state.

“Indeed Allah does not change a people’s lot, unless they change what is in their souls” gives the rationale for this preservation. God does not remove a people’s good condition until they alter their inward spiritual state—turning gratitude into ingratitude, obedience into disobedience, or faith into polytheism. A community that remains faithful, Godwary, grateful, and upright in accordance with fiṭra receives and retains blessings of this world and the Hereafter. When it abandons that inward uprightness, blessing may be changed into curse, guidance into misguidance, and happiness into misery.

The commentary rejects a reading that makes this a universal, reversible law by which every outward evil follows sin and every blessing follows renewed obedience. The context, especially “And when Allah wishes to visit ill on a people, there is nothing that can avert it,” concerns change from good to bad. God pardons many sins and erases their effects; thus, unlike the established connection between communal righteousness and the continuance of blessings, the verse does not make the descent of wrath upon a corrupt people an unconditional necessity. It permits such a change, and when God wills ill—after people have forsaken divine servanthood and the requirements of human nature—no misery, calamity, or punishment can be repelled, because they have no protector besides Him.

This applies principally to communities. For an individual, revelation connects righteous conduct with spiritual blessings and their loss when conduct changes, but does not connect individual righteousness with material prosperity. At the level of the human species, the connection between prevailing righteousness and general blessings follows from the teleological harmony of the cosmos: each species is equipped for its end, and human deviation from fiṭra and widespread corruption disrupt that harmony, bringing deprivation and corruption. This does not mean that each individual’s outward lot corresponds to his conduct, since individual purposes may fail without nullifying the divinely intended end of the species.

The verse also indicates that every aspect of a person—soul, body, traits, states, deeds, and effects—is entrusted to angelic preservation on the journey to God. A changing command lies in wait when people change themselves; among its effective sources is the appointed term, which is neither altered nor deferred. Preservation and change are distinct manifestations of one dominant divine command within an unchanging order.

The commentary rejects interpretations that make the pronoun refer to God or the Prophet because they require arbitrary shifts of referent and disrupt the context; it calls the interpretation of muʿaqqibāt as royal bodyguards especially untenable. It also rejects readings that limit “before and behind” to physical directions or to recorded past and future deeds, and readings that attach the verse to earlier references to punishment or to open daytime sin. The phrase is instead an exposition of “and everything is by measure with Him,” while the statement that God does not change a people’s lot explains the angels’ guarding by His command.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that yurī-kum means that God visibly shows lightning, while “He produces” describes His bringing forth the rain-laden clouds (saḥāb). “Inspiring fear and hope” means that lightning gives rise to both feelings: travelers or people at sea may fear it, while residents or people on land hope for its rain; people may also fear thunderbolts and hope for rain. The contrast between showing lightning and producing the laden clouds is part of the verse’s subtle eloquence.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains ṣawāʿiq as the superheated bolts descending from heaven that cause thunder. Jidāl is verbal disputation in which each side seeks to overcome the other, while miḥāl denotes vying in strength or seeking to outwit an opponent. The idolaters dispute God’s lordship by inventing arguments for their own gods and clinging to ancestral tradition, although God is great in might: He knows their deficiencies and is fully able to expose and humiliate them.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan explains that duʿāʾ and daʿwa are efforts, by speech or gesture, to direct the called person’s attention to the caller, while istijāba and ijāba are the called person’s turning toward the caller in response. A true invocation requires one who can attend to the caller and has both the will and capacity to respond. Calling one who neither understands nor can fulfill the need is only the appearance of a call.

“To Him belongs the true invocation (daʿwat al-ḥaqq)” therefore means that true, effective invocation belongs exclusively to God. He hears, is near, and responds; the verse makes genuine invocation and its response dependent only on directing the call to Him alone. Whether daʿwat al-ḥaqq is read adjectivally as the true call or literally as the invocation belonging to truth, the contrast is the same: God alone possesses the reality of invocation and response, because He alone is knowing and capable.

Those invoked besides God do not answer at all. Whether they are material idols without consciousness or the angels, jinn, stars, or human spirits imagined to stand behind them, they possess neither benefit nor harm, death, life, nor resurrection even for themselves. All dominion and power belong to God.

The image of someone extending his hands toward distant water to bring it to his mouth does not make a genuine exception to this denial; it intensifies it. A thirsty person must approach water and take it in hand to drink. One who merely reaches toward distant water has only the form of seeking and obtains no drop. Likewise, those who invoke others have only the empty form of invocation and receive nothing. Their invocations “only go awry” because God alone is the goal of invocation and turning toward Him alone is the path that reaches that goal. The interpretation of “the true invocation” as the profession that there is no god but God has no contextual support.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that sujūd, literally falling with the forehead or chin to the ground, also denotes the humility and abasement that such an act is meant to express. The Qurʾan accordingly attributes prostration, praise, invocation, and related acts to non-human beings. When attributed to creatures, their prostration and humility before God are real existential truths, not merely the conventional or figurative significance attached to human gestures.

The verse perhaps speaks primarily of rational beings in the heavens and earth, since its polemic addresses idolaters and summons them to prostrate willingly as other rational beings do. Yet the concluding reference to shadows indicates the universality of this abasement: every being is intrinsically dependent and submissive to its Sustainer. In this fundamental sense, creatures’ submission is voluntary, for no creature independently possesses anything by which to resist or rebel against God.

“Willingly or unwillingly (tawʿan wa karhan)” can nevertheless describe the condition of beings in the material world. What accords with a creature’s nature—life, survival, success, flourishing, and attaining its end—is welcomed and hence submitted to willingly. What opposes its nature—death, corruption, misfortunes, illness, or the nullification of its effects—is detested and thus submitted to unwillingly. In every case, however, creatures remain prostrate to God’s command.

The commentary rejects readings that reduce the verse to bodily prostration, with believers prostrating willingly and unbelievers through fear of the sword, or that make unbelievers’ unwilling submission merely their suffering of pain and illness. It also does not accept explanations that treat the prostration of created things as a bare allegory of existing as God wills.

The shadows of material bodies also prostrate in their existence and effects. Morning and evening are specified because shadows visibly lengthen and contract then, falling across the ground in a manner that displays the image of prostration; at midday they may be absent, slight, or apparently still. This is not empty poetry or mere imagination: the observable fall of shadows provides sensible minds with a true image through which to apprehend the intellectual reality of every being’s intrinsic prostration.

Likewise, thunder’s tremendous sound represents to hearing and imagination the intrinsic glorification that all beings express by their utter dependence on God, though that existential glorification is not conventional speech. More generally, when the Qurʾan points idolaters to phenomena whose causes are not apparent to sense, it does not confine God’s causality to the unknown while treating known causes as independent of Him. It affirms causality universally and directs reflection through causes to the First Cause, God.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan treats this verse as the epitome of the preceding argument. God alone creates, owns, governs, knows, sustains, and has power over the heavens, the earth, and everything in them. All others are created and governed, unable to possess benefit or harm even for themselves. He is therefore the sole Lord.

The Prophet is commanded to ask who is Lord of the heavens and earth and to answer, “Allah,” because the idolaters’ refusal of the oneness of lordship prevents them from grasping the argument. Once God’s lordship is established, their adoption of other guardians is self-refuting: beings unable to control their own benefit or harm cannot manage the affairs of others or possess the attributes of lordship. The rhetorical transition from commands to say certain conclusions to the question about blind and seeing, darkness and light, marks distance from people whose ignorance and obstinacy make direct engagement futile.

The blind and the seer, and darkness and light, contrast the faithless person who remains unmoved by manifest proofs with the believer who sees the truth. Faith and disbelief are not equal, and sound judgment should lead the idolaters to abandon falsehood and believe in the One God.

“Have they set up for Allah partners who have created like His creation, so that the creations seemed confusable to them?” is addressed in the third person to the Prophet, not put to the idolaters. They did not claim that another created the cosmos; they acknowledged God as its sole Creator. Their dispute with Islam concerned the oneness of lordship, not divine creation and origination. But God’s exclusive creation already refutes partners in lordship, since no other being can independently possess existence, knowledge, or power, and lordship cannot exist without these.

The question thus shows that the idolaters could sustain their claim only by alleging that their supposed gods created like God, which they do not allege. The command, “Allah is the creator of all things, and He is the One, the All-paramount,” decisively removes this possibility. God’s being One in creative power, conquering every number and multiplicity, proves that He has no partner; together, these attributes yield unicity (al-aḥadiyya). The commentary cautions against confusing this Qurʾanic proof of the oneness of lordship against polytheists with an argument for the existence of a Creator against atheists.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan explains (13:17) as a single composite parable of truth and falsehood, not two or three separate examples. God sends pure rain from above; valleys of differing capacities receive and carry it according to their capacities, while swelling foam rises on the torrent. Likewise, when metals and other materials are heated to make ornaments or useful wares, scum rises upon the molten substance. Both forms of scum disappear—when the flood dries or the metal cools—whereas the water and purified metal that benefit people remain.

The lexical details serve this meaning: awdiya are valleys or channels that gather rainwater; qadar is a capacity or measure; zabad is foam or surface impurity; jufāʾ is dross cast away; matāʿ is what is used or enjoyed; and makath is remaining over time. Al-Rāghib’s definition is retained: bāṭil is the opposite of ḥaqq and is what fails when tested against reality; it may concern statements or actions. Thus a belief is true when it corresponds to reality and false when it does not; an action is true when it achieves its intended end and false when it fails to do so. An existent is true insofar as it exists as believed, while what is nonexistent but supposed to exist is false. Even a real contingent thing is falsely conceived if it is imagined to possess independence or permanence that it does not have. In this sense, all things apart from God, and every passing luxury, are false.

The commentary holds that the phrase “That is how Allah compares the truth and falsehood” means that God establishes truth and falsehood in the same manner as the torrent and molten substance are established in contrast to their foam. Yaḍrib, literally “strikes,” here bears the sense of establishing or fixing, as in pitching a tent or erecting a wall; this underlies the expression ḍarab al-mathal, setting forth an exemplar for comparison. It therefore rejects the proposed ellipsis that God merely “sets forth the example” of truth and falsehood: the verse is complete without it, and its final words, “That is how Allah draws comparisons,” already explicitly state the drawing of comparisons.

The parable distinguishes what endures and benefits people in their worldly life and Hereafter from what is transient and null. Its final demonstrative may refer to the actual descent of rain, flowing of valleys, smelting, and arising of scum, not merely to statements about them. Its limitation occurs through the receptacles that receive it, each creature taking existence according to its capacity, preparedness, and capability. Such determinations, though they delimit the heavenly bounty, remain under God’s dominion and occur only by His permission.

Truth is from God, whereas falsehood is not attributed to Him, although it occurs by His permission. Every existent contains a fixed share of truth and returns to it as the false element is annulled; falsehood is bound to vanish.

Though the visible world contains struggle—such as fire and water opposing one another, or living things consuming one another—these things cooperate under the divine ordering to achieve their respective purposes, just as hammer and wood serve a carpenter, or the opposing sides of scales serve accurate weighing. True beliefs in the believer’s heart resemble life-giving water received according to capacity: they benefit people, revive hearts, and leave blessing. verses.18:
Al-Mizan reads al-ḥusnā, “the best,” as principally the best outcome or consequence of answering the Lord’s call, rather than merely the reward itself or Paradise, though the ultimate outcome includes divine blessing and Paradise. The succeeding description of the believers as receiving “the outcome of the ultimate abode: the Gardens of Eden” supports this reading.

Those who refuse the call face a consequence so tremendous, severe, and horrifying that, were they to possess everything on earth and as much again, they would offer it all to escape it. The unspecified object of their attempted ransom intensifies its indescribable horror; a tradition from Imām ʿAlī describes what will befall them as beyond description. Their adverse reckoning, sūʾ al-ḥisāb, is a reckoning that causes suffering and brings no happiness, and their refuge is hell. Mihād, ordinarily a laid-out resting place such as a mattress, calls hell a prepared resting place for disbelievers because of their disbelief and evil deeds.

The verse thus contrasts the good Hereafterly outcome of responding to the true divine call with the unwanted outcome of rejecting it, including severe judgment and a miserable abode. It develops the preceding parable of rain and valleys: responding to the call means accepting the invitation to faith, as valleys receive the descending water in accordance with their capacities.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan takes the question, “Is someone who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, like someone who is blind?” as a rhetorical denial of any equality between the two. Knowledge of revelation’s truth is insight, whereas ignorance of it is blindness. Those who possess intellect alone receive admonition, because they possess the hearts and intellect by which admonition is received; this explains why the knowing and the blind cannot be alike.

Truth settles in the hearts of those who answer their Lord, making them enlightened and giving them remembrance and insight. Their qualities are then detailed. They fulfill God’s covenant and do not break the solemn pledge. This means that they adhere to the covenant of their innate nature: recognizing God’s oneness and acting according to its moral implications. The covenants brought through prophets, religious laws, and divine ordinances all derive from this covenant of natural law, since religion rests upon natural law.

They also maintain whatever God has commanded to be joined. The command is apparently the legislative command communicated through revelation, since the following fear of adverse reckoning concerns accountability under revealed rules. Although some matters, such as the evil of oppression and goodness of justice, are recognized by natural disposition, a person who does not know God’s decree and is not culpable is not held accountable as one to whom revealed guidance has reached. Maintaining commanded bonds encompasses all divinely required relationships, with kinship among its foremost instances. Neglecting these bonds is disobedience and will be recorded as a bad deed.

The commentary distinguishes yakhshawn from yukhāfūn. Khashya is apparently the heart’s reverential response to apprehended evil, while khawf is fear that prompts precautionary action. Perhaps, as al-Rāghib holds, khashya is the stronger fear, joined with awe and rooted in knowledge. This distinction is necessary to avoid treating the two expressions as contradictory, even if usage does not always preserve it; the claim that there is no difference between them is rejected.

Their ṣabr is unrestricted and therefore includes patience in hardship, in obedience, and against sin. Yet it is qualified by seeking their Lord’s pleasure: only patience arising from response to God’s call and knowledge that revelation is true is praised here, not endurance motivated by pride or desire for praise. “Seeking their Lord’s countenance” means seeking the aspect in which deeds become manifest and are preserved with God as abiding reward. Maintaining prayer means making it enduring and not neglecting its parts, conditions, or importance; its particular mention after patience emphasizes its rank.

Their spending includes obligatory and non-obligatory expenditure. Since the verse is Meccan and zakāt had not yet been instituted, it is not confined to zakāt. Spending secretly or openly means using the form best suited to the case: it should be concealed where publicity risks ostentation, humiliation, or loss of dignity, and public where it encourages righteousness and good deeds. To repel evil with good is likewise comprehensive. It includes answering one’s own wrongdoing with good deeds and repentance, but also responding to others’ wrong with forgiveness, kindness, good manners, sound speech to the ignorant, prevention of hateful acts, and commanding what is right. Nothing in the wording confines it to one of these meanings.

Al-Mizan examines the shift between present-tense verbs for fulfilling, joining, fearing, and repelling, and past-tense verbs for patience, prayer, and spending. It rejects the explanation that this is merely stylistic variation in a conditional-like relative clause, because even when temporal specificity is removed, the past tense still conveys occurrence and the present still conveys continuation. It also rejects the view that the past tense merely marks the special importance of patience, prayer, and spending, since fulfillment of God’s covenant is not less important.

The commentary instead holds that patience, prayer, and spending together present the primary matter: performing good deeds through fulfilling duties and avoiding prohibitions. Repelling evil with good is supplementary, denoting compensation for shortcomings. The wording portrays those who possess intellect as established in every form of patience and continually watchful over their actions, promptly repairing any lapse in patience, prayer, or spending with good.

“The outcome of the ultimate abode” is the praiseworthy outcome that truly follows their deeds. Everything, according to the innate disposition upon which God created it, is directed toward an outcome suited to it and productive of happiness. A bad outcome is really the absence of that proper outcome due to a defect; calling it an outcome is figurative. Hence the verse leaves “outcome” unqualified: the true outcome is the good one. In contrast, the disbelievers are assigned “the ills of the abode,” not an outcome. The abode is accordingly the worldly abode, and the outcome of the ultimate abode is the final result of worldly life.

The Gardens of Eden are this ultimate abode. ʿAdn denotes settled, permanent residence, so these gardens signify stability, eternity, safety, and protection. Earthly life and the Hereafter are thus one continuous life: it begins amid pain and hardship in this world and reaches ease, blessing, and security at its end in the Hereafter. The entry of righteous forebears, spouses, and descendants with the believers corresponds to their maintaining the bonds God commanded them to maintain. The wording encompasses mothers through spouses, and broader relatives through forebears; it promises reunion with righteous kin.

verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that the angels’ greeting, “Peace be to you, for your patience. How excellent is the outcome of the abode!”, announces the culmination of the righteous deeds of those who remained steadfast in obedience, avoided sins, endured hardship, and lived with fear and awe of God. It reassures the possessors of intellect of everlasting security, peace, and good fortune, an outcome free from every defect and blame.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan contrasts the unbelievers with the faithful: they break God’s solemn covenant, sever what He commanded to be joined, and spread corruption in the earth. In opposition to this, righteous deeds alone reform the earth and produce the development and prosperity of human society, leading to the happiness and flourishing of humankind.

Their curse, al-laʿna, means being driven away and distanced from God’s mercy and grace. This is the consequence of disregarding truth and entering into falsehood, whose final result is only ruin and destruction; hence they receive the ills of the abode.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan explains that the favorable end and eternal Paradise of the possessors of intellect, as well as the curse and hell of covenant-breakers, are both forms of provision which God expands or restricts for whomever He wishes, without obligation or restriction upon Him. His bestowal accords with the enduring cosmic order of truth and falsehood: believing and acting upon truth brings the provisions of Paradise and eternal salvation, whereas believing and acting upon falsehood brings curse, hell, and a wretched life.

The real provision is that of the Hereafter. Covenant-breakers become absorbed in the outward adornment of worldly life, forget the Hereafter and its provision, and are content with what the world contains. Worldly life is a means for attaining the other life, not an end in itself. When used for the provision of eternal life, it has its proper place; when made an isolated end, it becomes a form of falsehood, vanishing without benefit like a dried riverbed.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that the faithless ask for another sign because they refuse to regard the revealed Qurʾan as a sign; had they regarded it as such, they would have followed it. The reply establishes that guidance does not result automatically from the appearance of signs, but belongs to Allah: He guides those who turn penitently to Him and leads astray those who turn away. This is not an arbitrary divine will, for His will follows a flawless order: repentance, truth-seeking, and freedom from the bondage of desire dispose a person to be guided through the Qurʾan, whereas attachment to desire causes even clear or miraculous signs to be of no benefit. Thus, “Allah leads astray whomever He wishes” means that by His will He leads astray those who do not turn to Him and guides those who do. The pronoun in yahdī ilay-hi refers to God Himself, not to the Qurʾan or the Messenger.

Al-Mizan takes (13:28) to explain the penitence of the preceding verse: those who turn to God are those who have faith and whose hearts find rest (taṭmaʾinnu) in His remembrance. Itmiʾnān is tranquility arising from reconciliation with something. Faith is not bare knowledge or intellectual assent, since one may know the truth while arrogantly denying it; it is the soul’s acceptance of what it knows, submission to its consequences, and the corresponding submission of one’s faculties and limbs. A person may recognize an act’s ugliness without abandoning it, but when that recognition is inwardly accepted, leaving the act becomes easier. Divine guidance therefore concerns the heart’s receptive acceptance: the opening of the breast to Islam is expressed here as faith and assurance, by which the matter becomes settled in the heart without agitation or retreat.

The clause about hearts finding assurance is consequently explanatory of faith, not an independent statement. It does not conflict with the trembling of faithful hearts when Allah is mentioned. Trembling and fear precede assurance: when the soul remembers God, it first sees its own deficiencies and fears that its evil deeds may cause divine mercy to be withheld; it then turns to its Lord, the object of its innate desire, and finds tranquility in His remembrance. Since all that proceeds from God is blessing, adversity is not a positive evil proceeding from Him but the withholding of blessing and mercy.

Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-bayān, distinguishes remembrance that recalls divine rewards and blessings, which brings ease, from remembrance that recalls punishment and vengeance, which brings fear. Al-Mizan judges that this better suits an interpretation of dhikr as the Qurʾan. It holds instead that remembrance includes verbal recitation and every attentiveness of thought and heart, whether through a sign, an argument, or a claim; the verse therefore states a universal principle, not one restricted to the Qurʾan.

Remembering Allah alone gives the heart its true security, because human beings seek happiness, salvation, and protection from misery, while all blessing, punishment, and affairs are under God’s control. Every heart finds relief from anxiety in His remembrance, except hearts so corrupted that they have lost their insight and no longer deserve to be called hearts. The word order in alā bi dhikr Allāh taṭmaʾinnu al-qulūb indicates exclusivity: only remembrance of God can truly give assurance. Any heart apparently at rest in something else is unaware of its real condition; were it aware, it would be overcome by anxiety. Al-Mizan rejects as strained the view that the verse begins a separate sentence whose predicate occurs in (13:29) and that the assurance clause is merely an interpolation.
verses.28:
Al-Mizan explains that the faithless ask for another sign because they refuse to regard the revealed Qurʾan as a sign; had they regarded it as such, they would have followed it. The reply establishes that guidance does not result automatically from the appearance of signs, but belongs to Allah: He guides those who turn penitently to Him and leads astray those who turn away. This is not an arbitrary divine will, for His will follows a flawless order: repentance, truth-seeking, and freedom from the bondage of desire dispose a person to be guided through the Qurʾan, whereas attachment to desire causes even clear or miraculous signs to be of no benefit. Thus, “Allah leads astray whomever He wishes” means that by His will He leads astray those who do not turn to Him and guides those who do. The pronoun in yahdī ilay-hi refers to God Himself, not to the Qurʾan or the Messenger.

Al-Mizan takes (13:28) to explain the penitence of the preceding verse: those who turn to God are those who have faith and whose hearts find rest (taṭmaʾinnu) in His remembrance. Itmiʾnān is tranquility arising from reconciliation with something. Faith is not bare knowledge or intellectual assent, since one may know the truth while arrogantly denying it; it is the soul’s acceptance of what it knows, submission to its consequences, and the corresponding submission of one’s faculties and limbs. verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains ṭūbā as the feminine comparative form derived from ṭayyib, qualifying an implicit “life” or “livelihood”: for the faithful who do righteous deeds is a purer, more virtuous life. Blessings are pleasant only insofar as they bring happiness and release the heart from anxiety, and such lasting tranquility belongs to those who believe, act righteously, and remember God. Having relied on the indestructible protection of God, they are safeguarded from evil and loss in what lies ahead: what they receive and what is withheld are both for their good.

The comparative sense may indicate that life is not wholly without purity, but that the life of those whose hearts are tranquil through God’s remembrance has a greater purity, being cleansed of the contamination of unpleasant experience. The precedence of ṭūbā over la-hum is congratulatory, bringing the cause for glad tidings immediately before the hearer. The verse thus promises believers who do righteous deeds a good life and a felicitous destination; this good life is an effect of their tranquil hearts.

Al-Ṭabrisī in Majmaʿ al-bayān reports explanations of ṭūbā as joy, happiness, goodness and honor, Paradise, a pleasant life, continuous blessing, or a tree in Paradise whose roots are in the Prophet’s abode and whose branches reach every believer’s house. Al-Mizan holds that most of these explanations are analogical rather than derived from the verse’s apparent sense.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan takes kadhālik to refer to the enduring divine way: nations are invited to monotheism, God guides or misguides according to His order, all things return to Him, and guidance belongs to faith, assurance in His remembrance, and not turning away. The Prophet is accordingly sent to recite the revelation to a nation preceded by perished nations, just as earlier messengers were sent, although this nation rejects the All-beneficent.

Their rejection of the Qurʾan, its ordinances, and their demand for another sign is called defiance of “the All-beneficent” because it is rejection of the principle of divine mercy itself—a mercy which, if accepted and acted on, would bring happiness in this world and the next. The Messenger is commanded to declare monotheism: Allah alone is his Lord, without partner; he trusts only Him and returns only to Him. Trust and return follow necessarily from Lordship, since the Lord owns and governs all affairs.

Matāb is an infinitive from tawba, “to return,” and means the return to God. Al-Mizan rejects the interpretation that makes it repentance from sins merely because its primary sense would supposedly only emphasize trust, and also rejects inserting the unsupported meaning that both the Messenger and his audience return to God.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains the demanded marvels as mountains uprooted and moved, the earth divided into pieces, and the dead restored to speech and questioned about their posthumous state. The verse addresses precisely such demands for signs, but its point is that even a Qurʾan producing these wonders would not guide these faithless people unless Allah willed. The conditional’s consequent is left implicit, while “Rather all dispensation belongs to Allah” rejects the assumption that an extraordinary sign would itself secure guidance. Guidance and misguidance belong wholly to God: He guides those who turn to Him and has led these opponents astray.

Al-Mizan rejects the view that the verse chiefly extols the Qurʾan’s eloquence and means that, if any recitation could move mountains, split the earth, or make the dead speak, it would be this Qurʾan. That reading does not fit “Rather all dispensation belongs to Allah” or “Have not the faithful yet realized that had Allah wished He would have guided mankind all together?” Nor do its proposed explanations of bal adequately connect the clauses. The proper reading is: even with such signs, they would not believe unless God willed.

Regarding a fa-lam yayʾasi, three explanations are reported. Some take yayʾasi, in a dialect, to mean “know”; others derive it from despair while holding that the interrogative implicitly includes knowledge; still others take it as literal despair without that implication. Al-Mizan prefers the second: the believers are to know that God has not willed these unbelievers’ guidance, though He could have guided all mankind, and to despair of their ever believing. The verse subtly addresses believers who had hoped that an additional sign might bring the disbelievers to faith and had urged the Messenger to answer their demand.

The catastrophes (qāriʿa) are disasters that portend something still worse. They are a warning that, because of their disbelief in the All-beneficent and opposition to Islam, the faithless will repeatedly suffer calamities themselves or near their dwellings until the promised punishment arrives; Allah does not break His promise. Al-Mizan identifies the faithless here with the Arab opponents of the early Islamic call, including the Meccans and others who reached the height of obstinacy and spread persecution and corruption. Calamities upon those around Mecca include war, killing, and plunder; calamities near Mecca include afflictions such as smoke, fear, grief, sleeplessness, and loss of sustenance. The promised punishment is the sword faced at Badr, Uḥud, and elsewhere.

This threat is not the general judgment promised to every nation in (10:47–54), but a specific warning to Quraysh and the other early opponents of the Messenger. In this unqualified Qurʾanic usage, “the faithless” denotes the Arab polytheists who first opposed Islam, while “the faithful” denotes the early Muslims who accepted its call.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan says that this verse reinforces the preceding, unequivocal threat by invoking an undeniable historical pattern: earlier messengers were mocked and disbelieved in, their peoples were granted respite, and then divine retribution seized them. The idolaters who reject the Qurʾan and demand signs tailored to their wishes should learn from those destroyed communities, change their conduct, and recognize that God’s punishment is neither an empty threat nor escapable or bearable.

The commentary therefore rejects the view that the verse is chiefly consolation or encouragement for the Messenger. Its pairing of messengers being derided with the faithless being given respite shows that mockery and disbelief are interchangeable here: their derision arose from disbelief, and their disbelief itself mocked God’s signs, just as the Prophet’s contemporaries denied the Qurʾan while mockingly asking why no sign had been sent down.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains qāʾim ʿalā as having control and authority over a thing, distinct from qāʾim bi, which denotes custody or management. God is qāʾim ʿalā every soul: He encompasses its essence, has power over it, and watches and witnesses it. He is also qāʾim ʿalā what each soul earns: He directs its deeds, records them, and transforms them into worldly and otherworldly reward or punishment, proximity or remoteness, guidance or misguidance, blessing or curse, Paradise or Hellfire. Since He alone governs every soul and its acts, no one can be equal to Him or worthy of partnership in divinity. Al-Mizan dismisses as alien to the context the attribution to Ḍaḥḥāk that the opening “who” refers to angels entrusted with human deeds.

“Name them!” demands that the idolaters identify attributes or effects that would establish their alleged partners’ divinity and intercessory standing. Yet idols have only such names as Hubal, Lāt, and ʿUzza, without any merit or attribute that qualifies them as partners. “Will you inform Him of something He does not know about on the earth?” exposes the implication of their claim: if a partner exercised any influence in creation, God could not be unaware of it. But God is the sole planner, and no influence or effect exists independently of Him. The phrase “or of (what are) mere words?” means that their assertion is an empty statement without reality; Al-Mizan rejects the alternative interpretation that it means a revealed book naming the idols.

The objection to idolatry thus has three connected aspects. The idolaters can point to no attributes proving their idols’ divinity; if they claim to have discovered such attributes, they falsely imply that they know of partners unknown to God; and if they are merely uttering words without truth, they are attempting to deceive God. Al-Zamakhsharī, in al-Kashshāf, is reported to have praised the striking force and eloquence of this argument.

The final “Rather” dismisses these supposed grounds altogether: Satan has made their idolatrous scheme attractive and barred them from God’s way. Al-Mizan states that they know they have no proof and promote idols for money and worldly adornment; because the Prophet’s mission obstructs these gains, they cling to idolatry in hostility and seek to mislead others. Satan adorns their scheme, while God has deprived them of guidance; whomever Allah leads astray has no guide.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains ashaqq as “harder,” from mashaqqa, hardship, and wāqq as a defender or protector, from wiqāya. The verse briefly specifies the punishment previously threatened to the faithless: they suffer punishment in this world, and the punishment of the Hereafter is harder. Having no defender against Allah means that no intercessor can benefit them under any circumstances.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains mathal as a description that fully represents what it describes. The verse contrasts the promise to the Godwary—Paradise with running streams and everlasting fruit and shade—with the threats against the faithless, thereby showing the final outcomes of the two paths in their return to God.

The contrast is between the faithless and the muttaqīn, not simply the faithful, because this excellent requital belongs to those who combine faith with righteous deeds. One who believes in God but does not act righteously is a believer in God yet a disbeliever in His signs. The alternation between “the Godwary” and “those who are Godwary,” and likewise between “the faithless” and “those who are faithless,” suggests that their established qualities and their past, collective deeds coincide in this context. Good deeds must therefore be performed consistently. The verse concerns two settled groups—those firmly persisting in disbelief and those firmly following faith—not people who repeatedly vacillate between faith and disbelief, whose beliefs and deeds have not settled on either path.

Al-Mizan further relates the varying forms of divine reference in the preceding verses to their contexts: “Thus have We sent you” points to mediated action through such means as angels and revelation; “Rather all dispensation belongs to Allah” indicates that every mediated and unmediated affair returns to God’s sustaining station; and “But then I gave respite to those who were faithless, then I seized them” negates the reality of any partner or intercessor. The final contrast between the requital of the Godwary and the Fire for the faithless concludes this discussion of believers and idolaters and of the effects of truth and falsehood upon belief and action.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan holds that “Those whom We have given the Book” apparently denotes the Jews and Christians, perhaps together with the Zoroastrians, as is customary Qurʾanic usage. Since the sūrah is Meccan, some Arabian Jews had not yet opposed the Prophet; some accepted his call and recognized him as the prophet foretold in their scriptures. Likewise, some Christians followed the true religion and did not oppose Islam, notably the Christians of Abyssinia and others; the foremost intended group appears to be such Christians, who held Jesus to be a human prophet sent by God, like Negus and his followers. The Zoroastrians too were awaiting the Seal of the Prophets and a religion of truth and justice and were not hostile in the manner of the polytheists. The command to worship Allah alone especially suits an address to Christians.

“The factions” (al-Aḥzāb), with its definite article, refers to known factions among the People of the Book. They reject part of the revelation: namely, verses affirming God’s oneness, rejecting the Trinity, and repudiating their false beliefs, corrupted knowledge, and distorted rulings. The Prophet’s declaration that he is commanded to worship Allah without associating partners shows that the denied part concerns unity in worship and obedience. His words, “To Him do I summon and to Him is my return,” declare both his aim and his path: he calls no one to other than God and refers all his affairs to Him. It is also possible that his return refers to resurrection, so that he calls solely to God because his return is solely to Him.

The commentary rejects the view that the Book is the Qurʾan, those given it are the Prophet’s Companions, and the factions are hostile Arab tribes: Qurʾanic usage does not specifically apply “Those whom We have given the Book” to the Companions, and the reading would needlessly repeat the following verse’s meaning. It also regards the interpretation confining the phrase to Jews and the Torah as strained, requiring elaborate arguments to explain how some Jews could rejoice in the Qurʾan while denying its contrary rulings. The views that “those” means all Muslims, that the factions are Jews, Christians, and Zoroastrians, or that the Prophet’s return implicitly includes theirs, lack support in the verse’s apparent wording.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that “thus” refers to the Book mentioned previously, including the scriptures revealed to earlier prophets such as the Torah and Gospel. The Qurʾan has been sent down as a ḥukm, meaning a divine judgment or verdict, and, correspondingly, a judge between people in their disputes; it does not mean ḥikma. “Arabic” qualifies this judgment and stresses that the Book was revealed in the Messenger’s own language, in accordance with God’s practice of sending each messenger in his people’s language. This also suggests that the People of the Book principally in view are Jews and Christians.

The warning against following “their desires” prohibits the Prophet from yielding to the People of the Book’s demands. They sought signs besides the Qurʾan, as did the idolaters, and considered abrogation of laws impossible, expecting the Messenger to follow their religious laws. Thus, he must neither desire an additional sign like the one they demand nor compromise by retaining any of their abrogated or distorted laws. If he did, no guardian or defender could save him from God’s punishment. The address is directed specifically to God’s Messenger, not to the community generally.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that, after the Prophet is forbidden to follow the People of the Book’s desires concerning additional signs, the verse recalls the true condition of messengers and directs him to rely on God in all affairs. God’s established way is to choose human messengers from among people, with wives and descendants, not beings who control the unseen or possess divine independence and unrestricted supernatural power. They have no authority over their own affairs; all authority belongs to God.

Signs and miracles come only by Allah’s leave, and He grants them only when wisdom requires it, not whenever they are requested, lest the divine order be disrupted. Every period has its appropriate wisdom, decree, and sign. “There is a decree for every term” therefore means that each time has a prescribed decree and each decree its appointed time; nothing occurs except what is written in that decree. The interpretation that the phrase means each revealed book—the Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾan—has its own period is rejected as unworthy of consideration.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that yamḥū means removing a thing’s trace completely and is synonymous with naskh, or abrogation. Yuthbit, from ithbāt, is its opposite: preserving or fixing a thing in its place. Since “Allah effaces and confirms whatever He wishes” is joined both to “There is a decree for every term” and to “with Him is the Mother Book,” a decree or book affirmed at one time may be effaced later and another confirmed in its place. If the contents of the book are taken as divine signs and indications, and all existents are signs of God, then God continually effaces one sign and confirms another.

The verse explains why every time has its particular book or decree: books differ with differing times because God Himself effaces what He wills and confirms another in its place, not because the books possess an independently fixed and unalterable condition. “The Mother Book” means the origin and essence of the book, for umm denotes that from which something proceeds and to which it returns. It is the immutable, foundational decree to which the changing decrees return. Without it, effacement and confirmation would either depend on external causes, making God constrained by them, or be arbitrary, destroying the ordered and purposeful system of creation. Thus God may replace a settled decree at one time with another at a later time, while every moment nevertheless has an unchangeable foundational decree.

This rule of effacement and confirmation is general, extending to everything in the heavens, the earth, and what lies between them; the immediate context of prophetic signs does not restrict its scope. The commentary consequently rejects attempts to confine the verse to particular cases, such as legal abrogation, records of deeds, forgiveness or persistence of sins, the effects of prayer and almsgiving, repentance, the replacement of generations, night and day, this world and the next, sleep, or decrees on the Night of Decree. Such interpretations lack textual evidence for exclusivity.

Observation itself shows this generality: things change across time in their essences, attributes, and acts, yet each state, considered in its own actual reality, is stable and does not change from its own nature. Observable things therefore have a dimension of change—life, death, cessation, permanence, and transformation—and a dimension of stability; these correspond to, or derive from, the Book of Erasure and Confirmation and the Mother Book.

God also has a fixed decree for everything that admits no change. Reports and supplications concerning prayer or almsgiving averting adversity, including prayers to be erased from wretchedness and inscribed among the fortunate, concern only non-definitive decrees (al-qaḍāʾ ghayr al-maḥtūm). Divine decree is therefore divided into a mutable decree (qaḍāʾ mutaghayyir) and an immutable decree (qaḍāʾ ghayr mutaghayyir).
verses.40: Al-Mizan notes that in is conditional and mā is added for emphasis, as indicated by the emphatic nūn in nuriyyanna-ka. The verse defines the Prophet’s duty as warning and communicating the message. He must not follow people’s desires concerning the sign they demand, nor expect necessarily to witness either the outcome of his mission or the punishment promised to them. Reckoning belongs to God, and the verse indicates that divine reckoning occurs in this world as well as in the hereafter.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan explains that the rhetorical question calls its hearers to reflect after being threatened with destruction. God’s “visiting” the land and diminishing it at its edges figuratively means bringing death and destruction upon its inhabitants.

The interpretation that it foretells Muslims conquering villages around Mecca, progressively reducing Meccan territory, is rejected because this is a Meccan sūrah and those conquests occurred only after the Emigration to Medina. The threats do, however, foreshadow the Meccans’ destruction at Badr and other battles, rather than the conquest of Mecca.

“Allah judges, and there is none who may repeal His judgment” means that all dominance belongs to Him: none can reverse, prevent, or overcome His judgment. He reckons every deed as soon as it occurs, without delay or opportunity for interference.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that earlier peoples plotted, but their schemes did not benefit them or prevent God from visiting the land and diminishing it at its edges. Allah encompasses every plot, nullifies it, and turns it back upon its plotters as a lesson. His knowledge of what every soul earns demonstrates this control, for a plot succeeds only against one ignorant of it; once it is known, it is defeated.

The declaration that the faithless will soon know for whom the outcome of that abode is decisively affirms an inevitable result which they will witness themselves. There is therefore no need to prolong the warning: they will soon come to know it.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains that the chapter answers those who rejected the Qur’an as the sign of the Prophet’s mission and demanded another sign. When no alternative sign was given, they denied prophethood itself, saying, “You have not been sent.” The reply, “Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and he who possesses the knowledge of the Book,” is therefore a decisive proof, not a merely rhetorical appeal to knowledge unavailable to the opponents.

Allah’s testimony here is an assertive declaration of the Prophet’s mission, of the kind found in the Qur’an’s declaration, “you are indeed one of the messengers, on a straight path” (36:3). Some commentators take the divine testimony to mean God’s establishment of compelling proofs, treating the act of adducing evidence metaphorically as testimony. Although this reaches the intended conclusion, Al-Mizan holds that it takes the wrong route. The relevant proof in this chapter is the Qur’an itself: it is both an enduring miracle and God’s speech testifying to the Prophet’s mission. Since the Qur’an is speech as well as a miraculous sign, God’s testimony need not be construed as a metaphor referring to His other acts; nor is His action inherently stronger evidence than His speech. Thus, “Allah suffices as a witness between me and you” means that what the Qur’an says affirming the prophetic mission is God’s own attestation to it.

“Testimony” cannot mean merely bearing witness in the sense of seeing or knowing an event. To argue with opponents from God’s private knowledge would not establish anything for them, since they cannot access that knowledge to determine whether the Messenger speaks truthfully or falsely attributes words to God. The testimony must instead be a declaration accessible in the Qur’an.

Al-Mizan rejects the view that “he who possesses the knowledge of the Book” means God, with “the Book” understood as the preserved tablet. This conflicts with the apparent conjunction: after Allah has already been named as sufficient witness, the clause should not simply repeat Him. It also inelegantly joins God’s essence to an attribute of His essence. Al-Zamakhsharī, transmitting al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī’s view, attempted to resolve this by paraphrasing Allah as “the One worthy of worship” and the relative pronoun as “the one,” so that two attributes are conjoined. But a paraphrase that yields a direct meaning cannot make the original wording sound. On the proper understanding, “Allah” denotes God’s very essence, possessing all perfection, whose testimony surpasses every other testimony; this accords with: Say, ‘W hat thing is greatest as witness?’ Say, ‘Allah is the witness between me and you...’ (6:19).

The commentary also rejects identifying “the Book” with the Torah, the Gospel, or the Torah alone, and the witness with their learned followers who knew prophecies and descriptions of the Prophet. The verse concerns actual attestation, not mere knowledge, while this is a Meccan chapter and no scholar of the People of the Book had then believed and testified. The proposal that it means later Muslim converts such as ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām, Tamīm al-Dāri, al-Jārūd, or Salmān al-Fārsī fails because they embraced Islam after the migration to Medina.

The possibility that this particular verse was Medinan, despite the chapter being Meccan, proves nothing without a reliable narration. Moreover, commentators explicitly regard the chapter as Meccan, and although Medinan verses may occur within Meccan chapters, this verse concludes the chapter and is connected with its opening; such connected verses cannot plausibly have been separated by years. Nor can a Meccan verse answer its contemporary deniers by telling them to accept the Prophet without present evidence because later scholars would testify. The contention that a witness need only possess knowledge, not faith, is equally unsound: if unacknowledged knowledge of the People of the Book could establish the case, the alleged knowledge of the disbelievers themselves could also be invoked, although both groups denied the mission. Again, the testimony is an attestation, not simply awareness. Al-Mizan likewise dismisses Ibn Taymiyya’s claim that the entire verse was Medinan as unsupported.

A further interpretation makes “the Book” the Qur’an: one who truly knows and is responsible for it testifies that it is from God and that the Prophet was sent with it. This coheres with the chapter’s opening, “These are the signs of the Book. That which has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe” (13:1), and its central statement, “Is someone who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth, like someone who is blind? Only those who possess intellect take admonition” (13:19). The verse thus defends the Qur’an against those who demanded a sign and denied the Messenger, and its form itself strongly indicates that it belongs to the Meccan chapter.

This understanding supports the numerous reports, from various sources and from the Imāms of the Ahl al-Bayt (peace be upon them), that the verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī. If “he who possesses the knowledge of the Book” referred to any believer then present, he would have to be the community’s most knowledgeable person regarding God’s Book; numerous authentic reports support this. Al-Mizan also invokes the widely transmitted Ḥadīth al-Thaqalayn, narrated by Sunni and Shiʿi sources, in which the Prophet leaves “The Book of God (Kitāb Allāh) and my progeny, the People of my House (ʿItratī Ahl Baytī),” declaring that they “shall never part until they come to me by the Pool” and that holding to both prevents going astray.
